name: Sikkimese
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Yliniemi, Juha 2019. A descriptive grammar of Denjongke (Sikkimese Bhutia), U. Helsinki PhD (phonology chapter plausibly covers stress); helda.helsinki.fi blocked access

new_statements.quote: I have not found stress to be a useful category for describing Denjongke. [...] There are, however, two reasons for not considering the pitch difference in disyllabic nouns in Denjongke as constituting stress. The first is that, Denjongke is sensitive to how much the pitch rises from the first syllable to the second one in disyllabic words (see §2.6.2), a distinction that is better described in terms of tone than stress. Second, the correlates of stress (pitch, intensity, vowel duration, vowel quality) are inconsistently pronounced in disyllabic words, especially when comparing words pronounced in context with those pronounced in isolation.
new_statements.citation: Yliniemi, Juha. 2021. A descriptive grammar of Denjongke (Sikkimese Bhutia). Himalayan Linguistics Archive 10. Santa Barbara: University of California. doi:10.5070/H920146466 (identical wording in the 2019 Helsinki PhD, §2.7, pp. 64-65)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Denjongke is a two-register (high/low) tone language (register largely predictable from the initial consonant, pitch decisive in some minimal pairs). The author explicitly declines to posit word stress: disyllabic nouns in clausal context show a low-high pitch pattern (higher pitch on the second syllable), but this is analysed as the tonal pitch-rise contrast, not stress, and the usual stress correlates are inconsistent between isolation and context. In verbs the tone sits on the monosyllabic root (first syllable); verbal suffixes are tonally neutral and take pitch from intonation. The 2005 MA thesis (§5.6, p. 59) says the same more bluntly: stress 'seems to be a non-significant category in Denjongka words'.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; the author notes that in isolation the first syllable of high-tone disyllabic nouns is sometimes at equal pitch with the second, and that the verb suffix -di/ti may be higher or lower in pitch than the root depending on intonation (§2.7, §16.7).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (disyllabic nouns and verb root + suffix), compared in isolation vs. carrier-sentence context; based on instrumental (Praat) study of 29 disyllabic nouns with one speaker plus other speakers (§2.6.2).
new_statements.identity_note: Denjongke / Sikkimese Bhutia / Lhoke = Sikkimese sikk1242 (ISO sip); Yliniemi describes the language of Sikkim generally (fieldwork with speakers from several parts of Sikkim), not a single named dialect. Sandberg's 'Sikkim-Bhutia / Dé-jong Ké' is the same language. The LSI 'Bhotia' sketches (Sikkim, West Bengal) cover the same language as spoken in Sikkim and the Darjeeling hills.

sources.note: §2.7 'Stress or tone', pp. 65-66 (PDF 97-98): stress is not a useful descriptive category; the higher pitch on the 2nd syllable of disyllabic nouns in context is analysed as tone/register (degree of pitch rise, §2.6.2), not stress, and stress correlates are inconsistent between isolation and context; tone in verbs sits on the monosyllabic root, suffixes are tonally neutral.

sources.citation: Yliniemi, Juha. 2005. Preliminary phonological analysis of Denjongka of Sikkim. MA thesis, University of Helsinki. 75 pp. hdl:10138/19355
sources.note: §5.6 'Stress', pp. 59-60: 'Stress, defined as prominence due to intensity, vowel duration, vowel quality and pitch, seems to be a non-significant category in Denjongka words. It is difficult to find consistent stress patterns in multisyllabic words'; cues conflict and vary between repetitions; compared to Kagate (Hoehlig & Hari 1976) and Lhomi (Vesalainen & Vesalainen 1976). Elsewhere (p. ~24) mentions /a/ lowering 'in unstressed second syllables in disyllabic words'.
